name: Valkey
summary: The Linux Foundation’s BSD-licensed fork of Redis 7.2.4: an in-memory key-value server that Redis clients can talk to unchanged.
intro: Valkey keeps its whole dataset in RAM and answers commands over the same protocol as Redis, with the same data types: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets and streams. Valkey 8 is fully compatible with Redis OSS 7.2.4, so existing clients, tools and data files work as they are. Persistence works the same way too: periodic RDB snapshots, or an append-only file that with the default once-a-second `fsync` can lose about a second of writes. In cluster mode keys are spread over 16,384 slots, each shard has a primary and replicas, and replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose writes that were already acknowledged. JSON, Bloom filters, vector and full-text search, and LDAP login come as separate modules, packaged together in `valkey-bundle`.

Since Valkey 8.0 the main thread hands network reads and writes to I/O threads and spends its own time executing commands, which lifted one server from about 380,000 to 1.2 million requests per second on AWS r7g machines. Valkey 9.0 moves whole slots between nodes atomically during resharding, lets hash fields expire one by one, allows numbered databases in cluster mode, and scales clusters to 2,000 nodes; 9.1 reaches 2.1 million requests per second on one server. Amazon ElastiCache and MemoryDB, Google Cloud Memorystore, Aiven and DigitalOcean all sell it as a managed service, and on AWS Valkey costs less than the Redis OSS engine.
strengths: BSD-3-Clause under the Linux Foundation, with a technical steering committee where no organisation may hold more than a third of the seats
A drop-in replacement for Redis OSS 7.2: same commands, protocol, clients and data files, and ElastiCache upgrades a Redis OSS cache to Valkey in place without downtime
Cheaper managed hosting on AWS: ElastiCache nodes cost 20% less and serverless 33% less than Redis OSS, and MemoryDB writes the first 10 TB a month free
I/O threads use more CPU cores while commands still run one at a time, so a single server reaches 1.2 to 2.1 million requests per second
limits: It splits from Redis at 7.2.4: features Redis added later, such as vector sets and the built-in Query Engine and time series of Redis 8, aren’t in Valkey, so apps that use them can’t switch back and forth
JSON, Bloom, search and LDAP are separate modules: you load them or run `valkey-bundle`, and managed services choose which ones they offer (Memorystore supports a subset of commands)
The usual in-memory trade-offs remain: data must fit in RAM, the default AOF setting can lose a second of writes, and cluster failover can lose acknowledged writes
Microsoft doesn’t run Valkey: Azure Managed Redis is built on Redis Enterprise, so on Azure Valkey means a third party such as Aiven

snippet.title: Run Valkey 9.1 with I/O threads and try commands added since the fork
source: # a lock that only its owner can release (DELIFEQ, Valkey 9.0)
vk SET lock:invoice:1042 worker-7 NX PX 30000
# one hash field expires on its own while the rest stays (HSETEX, Valkey 9.0)
vk HSETEX user:17 EX 300 FIELDS 1 otp 482913
vk HTTL user:17 FIELDS 2 otp name
# compare-and-set on a string (SET ... IFEQ, Valkey 8.1)
vk SET config:version v2 IFEQ v1

sections.title: Valkey or Redis today?
sections.intro: Both grew from the same code until March 2024. Versions checked on GitHub on 2026-10-06.

sections.title: Where to run it managed
sections.intro: On-demand list prices for one node of about 13 GB, checked 2026-10-06 (AWS: US East, N. Virginia; Google Cloud: Iowa). A highly available setup needs at least one replica, so double them.

items.name: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey
items.text: A `cache.r7g.large` node (13.07 GiB) costs $0.1752 an hour, against $0.219 for Redis OSS. Serverless caches cost $0.084 per GB-hour plus $0.0023 per million ECPUs, with a 100 MB minimum (about $6 a month). Valkey 9.0 and later can add a durable Multi-AZ log.

items.name: Amazon MemoryDB for Valkey
items.text: Stores data durably in a Multi-AZ transactional log, so failover and restarts don’t lose it. A `db.r7g.large` Valkey node costs $0.2163 an hour against $0.309 for Redis OSS, and the first 10 TB written each month are free (then $0.04 per GB).

items.name: Google Cloud Memorystore for Valkey
items.text: Shards with up to five replicas each, in Cluster Mode Enabled or Disabled, on Valkey 7.2, 8.0, 9.0 or 9.1. A `highmem-medium` node (13 GB) costs $0.1923 an hour, billed per second; one- and three-year commitments cut that by 20% and 40%.

items.name: Aiven and DigitalOcean
items.text: Aiven runs managed Valkey on several clouds. DigitalOcean replaced its Managed Redis with Managed Caching for Valkey.

story: For fifteen years Redis’s core was BSD-licensed, and cloud providers sold it as managed services. On 20 March 2024 Redis Ltd. announced that from version 7.4 Redis would be available only under RSALv2 or SSPLv1, saying the largest cloud providers commoditised its investment; they would now need a licence deal to offer new versions.

Eight days later the Linux Foundation announced Valkey, picking up development from Redis 7.2.4 under the BSD licence, backed by AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, Ericsson and Snap. It was led by former Redis contributors, among them Madelyn Olson of AWS, who had been on Redis’s core team, Ping Xie of Google Cloud and Viktor Söderqvist of Ericsson. The first stable release, 7.2.5 in April 2024, only renamed things. Valkey 8.0 in September brought multithreaded I/O, and within weeks AWS offered Valkey on ElastiCache and MemoryDB at lower prices than Redis OSS.

In May 2025 Redis added the open-source AGPLv3 as a third licence option for Redis 8. By then the two had drifted apart, and Valkey 9.0 in October 2025 shipped features Redis doesn’t have, such as numbered databases in cluster mode.

choices.why: Keeping the BSD licence meant anyone, cloud providers included, could keep using, distributing and selling the software without a licence deal.

choices.choice: A foundation with a seat cap per company
choices.why: A project held by a foundation rather than one company can’t be relicensed by surprise; the governance rules let no organisation hold more than a third of the steering committee.
Users could switch without changing code. Valkey 8.0 made no backwards-incompatible changes to command syntax or responses.

choices.choice: I/O threads around a single command thread
choices.why: The main thread hands network work to I/O threads and keeps running commands itself, orchestrating every job so that no race conditions occur, while more cores take the I/O load.
